---

## Abstract

**Background:** Epilepsy is among the most treatable neurological disorders, yet
most affected people in low-resource settings go untreated. Whether Africa's
share of epilepsy *trial* activity matches its disproportionate epilepsy *burden*
has not been quantified against a registry baseline.

**Methods:** Full-registry AACT April-12-2026 analysis. Trials were counted as
"epilepsy" if a condition term matched epilepsy/epileptic/seizure-disorder, and
as "African-site" if ≥1 facility country was among the 54 African Union states.
The metric is the within-disease African share, benchmarked to the 4.33%
registry-wide African-site rate. Burden and treatment-gap figures were taken from
PubMed-verified primary sources.

**Results:** 2,103 global epilepsy trials; **72 (3.42%) include an African site**
(1,469 interventional; 54 African = 3.68%) — *below* the 4.33% all-disease
baseline. This under-representation coincides with an epilepsy burden that is
overwhelmingly concentrated in low-resource settings: active-epilepsy prevalence
is roughly 12.7 per 1,000 in rural developing-country populations versus 4.9 per
1,000 in developed countries [4]; ~80% of people with epilepsy live in developing
countries [6]; and the pooled epilepsy treatment gap in developing countries is
about 56% (12 of the analysed studies were African) [5].

**Conclusion:** Africa carries a disproportionate epilepsy burden and a ~56%
treatment gap, yet under 4% of the world's epilepsy trials include an African
site — below even the low baseline share of African participation across all
diseases. The evidence base guiding epilepsy care is generated largely where the
disease is least concentrated.

---

## 1. Introduction

Epilepsy affects tens of millions worldwide and, unlike many chronic conditions,
is highly responsive to inexpensive first-line antiseizure medicines — yet in
low-resource settings the majority of people with epilepsy receive no appropriate
treatment, a phenomenon termed the **treatment gap** [5]. Two structural facts
frame this paper. First, epilepsy burden is concentrated in developing countries:
active-epilepsy prevalence is markedly higher in rural developing settings than
in developed countries [4], and roughly 80% of affected people live in developing
countries [6]. Second, the therapies and much of the trial evidence originate in
high-income settings. We ask whether African trial activity in epilepsy is
commensurate with African burden, using a full-registry denominator.

---

## 2. Methods

**Data.** AACT April-12-2026 flat-file snapshot; records reassembled by start
signature before field splitting (AACT text fields embed newlines).
**Epilepsy trials.** `conditions.downcase_name` containing "epilepsy",
"epileptic", or "seizure disorder" (distinct nct_ids).
**African-site trial.** ≥1 `facilities.country` among the 54 AU member states;
registry-wide this is 25,125 trials (4.33%).
**Metric.** Within-disease African share = African-site epilepsy trials ÷ global
epilepsy trials, compared to the 4.33% baseline.
**Burden/treatment-gap figures.** From PubMed-verified sources [4,5,6]; not
re-derived here.

---

## 3. Results

### 3.1 African share of epilepsy trials (AACT 2026-04-12)

| Metric | Global | African-site | African share |
|---|---|---|---|
| All epilepsy trials | 2,103 | 72 | **3.42%** |
| Interventional only | 1,469 | 54 | 3.68% |
| Registry baseline (all diseases) | 579,828 | 25,125 | 4.33% |

Epilepsy's African trial share (3.42%) sits **below** the already-low
all-disease baseline (4.33%) — i.e. epilepsy is *not* a disease for which African
sites are over-represented, despite the burden concentration. Only 72 of 2,103
global epilepsy trials touch an African site.

### 3.2 Burden and treatment gap (verified literature)

| Quantity | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Active-epilepsy prevalence, rural developing countries | ~12.7 / 1,000 | Ngugi 2010 [4] |
| Active-epilepsy prevalence, developed countries | ~4.9 / 1,000 | Ngugi 2010 [4] |
| Share of people with epilepsy in developing countries | ~80% | Birbeck 2010 [6] |
| Pooled treatment gap, developing countries | ~56% (95% CI 31–100) | Mbuba 2008 [5] |
| African studies in that treatment-gap synthesis | 12 of 27 | Mbuba 2008 [5] |

The juxtaposition is the finding: prevalence is ~2.5× higher in rural developing
settings, ~80% of the burden is in developing countries, and more than half of
people with epilepsy there are untreated — yet under 4% of the world's epilepsy
trials include any African site.

---

## 4. Discussion

The epilepsy portfolio illustrates a distinctive inequity. Epilepsy is not a
"neglected tropical disease" with a near-zero trial base; it has a substantial
global trial enterprise (2,103 trials). The inequity is *distributional*: that
enterprise is sited overwhelmingly outside the regions where epilepsy is most
prevalent and most under-treated. The consequence is that questions of specific
relevance to African epilepsy care — the aetiological contribution of endemic
infections (for example, the association between toxoplasmosis and epilepsy [7]
and other parasitic/CNS-infective causes over-represented in Africa), optimal
first-line antiseizure-medicine selection under supply constraints, task-shifted
delivery through primary care, and adherence in settings with intermittent drug
availability — are under-studied relative to their importance.

The treatment gap (~56%) is driven by shortages of skilled personnel, treatment
cost, cultural beliefs, and unreliable antiseizure-medicine supply [5]. These are
precisely the factors best addressed by pragmatic implementation trials conducted
*in* the affected settings — the kind of trial least represented in the current
African epilepsy portfolio. Birbeck's framing [6] is apt: cost-effective,
sustainable epilepsy care delivered through existing primary-health facilities,
supported by neurologists acting as educators and advocates, can close much of
the gap — but building that evidence requires African trial infrastructure.

The proportional-versus-absolute distinction matters. Africa's 3.42% share of
epilepsy trials is not merely "low relative to burden"; it is below the 4.33%
baseline share Africa holds across *all* diseases, so epilepsy is, if anything,
*relatively* de-prioritised for African trial siting even within an already
inequitable global system.

---

## 5. Limitations

Registry counts undercount trials registered only on PACTR or national African
registries not mirrored in ClinicalTrials.gov, so the true African epilepsy-trial
count may be modestly higher. Condition keyword matching may miss trials where
epilepsy is a secondary condition. Prevalence and treatment-gap figures carry
wide reported ranges (the treatment-gap CI spans 31–100%) reflecting genuine
between-study heterogeneity [4,5]. African-site counting credits any trial with
≥1 African facility, which may over-credit large multinational trials that enrol
few African participants; the true participant-weighted share is likely lower
still. Registry-visible siting does not by itself establish an evidence deficiency
for every clinical question.

---

## 6. Conclusion

Of 2,103 global epilepsy trials, only 72 (3.42%) include an African site — below
the 4.33% baseline African share across all diseases — even though active-epilepsy
prevalence is ~2.5× higher in rural developing settings, ~80% of people with
epilepsy live in developing countries, and the developing-country treatment gap
is ~56%. Africa bears a disproportionate, highly treatable epilepsy burden while
being under-represented in the trials that generate epilepsy evidence. Closing
the gap requires pragmatic, African-sited implementation trials of task-shifted,
primary-care-delivered antiseizure treatment.
